passage: "You've barely touched your dinner, Jatin," Amandeep said, and sat beside his nephew on the balcony step. "Rohan and the others stopped calling you, didn't they?" Jatin shrugged. "I'll tell you about the year my own group split. I was sixteen. I stopped answering the door and wrote half-sentences on the back wall of my room, things only I understood. Then I rode my bicycle until my legs shook, every single evening." He smiled a little. "It felt like the whole world had ended. My mother never asked me to snap out of it. She left tea outside my door. A cousin dropped by and sat on my floor with me. That helped more than anything he said."

qa.q: What did Amandeep write on the back wall of his room?
qa.a: He wrote half-sentences that only he understood.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling in the year his group split?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and very sad, shown by not answering the door, riding his bicycle until his legs shook, and feeling that the whole world had ended.

qa.q: How could Jatin's family support him right now?
qa.a: They could stay nearby without hurrying him, listen when he wants to talk, and invite him for small activities, as Amandeep's mother and cousin did.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's mother have felt while leaving tea outside the door?
qa.a: She was probably worried and wanted to help, but chose to give him space and quiet care instead of pushing him to feel better. 🤍

grounding: A teen after a friend group split withdraws and throws himself into activity, and family support helps recovery.

passage: Snow fell sideways across the village court, and the power had gone out an hour ago. Dolma kept running drills on the cold ground long after the other players went home, her breath white. That morning she had changed her status to a single line: "some doors close quietly." Nobody had asked what it meant. Anirban, the goalkeeper, had seen it on his cracked phone screen, and now he stood at the edge of the court with a torch, waiting for her to notice him. When she finally stopped, he said, "I'm not asking you to explain. Want to run or sit?" Dolma looked at the dark hills. "Sit," she said. "Just for a bit."

qa.q: What did Dolma write in her status?
qa.a: She wrote a single line: 'some doors close quietly.'

qa.q: What might Dolma be feeling as she keeps running the drills?
qa.a: She is probably hurting and trying to outrun it through activity, and her cryptic status suggests she wants to be noticed without having to explain; another reading is that she simply needed exercise.

qa.q: What could Anirban do after she sits down?
qa.a: He can stay beside her, listen if she wants to talk, and let her go at her own pace without pushing for details.

qa.q: Why might Anirban have come with a torch rather than messaging her?
qa.a: He saw that she was still out in the dark and cold, and being physically there shows care that a message could not, especially when the phone signal is poor.

grounding: After a breakup or split a teen withdraws, posts a cryptic line and throws herself into activity, and a friend's support begins recovery.

passage:
After the fight in the lunch queue, Reena's friend group of five became a group of four, and Reena wasn't in it. That night she posted a single line on her status: "Some people show their true colours eventually." Then she turned her phone off.
For a week she came straight home from school in their Thane building and shut her door. She stopped going down to the courtyard.
Her older sister Arohi noticed the door and the status. On Saturday she knocked with chai.
"I saw your status. Want to tell me about it, or just drink this?"
Reena drank half the cup in silence. Then it poured out: the group chat without her, the photo from the birthday she wasn't invited to.
Arohi listened, and didn't call them worthless. She said, "That sounds so lonely."
That evening their mother took them both out for pani puri, and Reena laughed for the first time in a week.

qa.q: What line did Reena post on her status?
qa.a: "Some people show their true colours eventually."

qa.q: What was Reena feeling during that week?
qa.a: Reena felt heartbroken and lonely after being cut out of her friend group, and was withdrawing from everyone.

qa.q: What made Arohi's support work?
qa.a: She noticed the signs, offered chai without pressure, listened, and named the loneliness instead of dismissing the friends.

qa.q: How might Reena's mother have seen the week?
qa.a: She likely noticed Reena's withdrawal too and chose a small, warm outing to help her reconnect.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager withdrawing and posting a cryptic message after a friend group split, and family support helping.

"Ojas, you've run every morning this week. And stayed back for extra practice every evening."
"Yeah. Training for the district meet."
"The meet's in March. It's October."
Ojas kept retying his shoelace. "So I'm early."
Aditi sat down on the track beside him. "You've done that lace three times."
He stopped.
"Is this about Kavya?"
"We broke up. Last Friday." His voice was flat. "If I stop moving, I think about it. So I don't stop."
"That sounds exhausting."
"It is." He rubbed his face. "It feels like the whole thing is sitting on my chest."
"You don't have to run it off alone. Want to get food after? Just food. No talking unless you want."
He nodded. "My mum keeps making my favourite rajma. I think she's noticed."
"Then let her notice," Aditi said. "And let me too."

qa.q: When is the district meet?
qa.a: The meet's in March.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling after the breakup?
qa.a: Ojas felt overwhelmed and heartbroken, as if it were sitting on his chest, and kept busy to avoid thinking about it.

qa.q: What did Aditi do that helped?
qa.a: She noticed he was overdoing activity, asked gently about the breakup, named how exhausting it sounded, and offered company without pressure.

qa.q: How might Ojas's mum be showing support?
qa.a: She seems to have noticed his sadness and is quietly caring for him by making his favourite rajma.

grounding: The dialogue shows a teenager throwing himself into activity after a breakup and friends and family helping him recover.

passage:
When Francis and I broke up at sixteen, I thought I'd never feel normal again. It had been eight months, which felt like forever. He said he just wanted to focus on exams. Everyone said it was mutual. It wasn't.
For two weeks I didn't eat breakfast. I deleted every photo, then undeleted them at midnight. I posted sad lyrics with no caption. I stopped going to dance class.
My mother didn't lecture. One night she sat at the end of my bed and said, "I'm not going to say he's not worth it. I know you loved him. That hurts."
I cried till I couldn't breathe properly. She just stayed.
The next weekend my friends turned up with a terrible film and too much popcorn. Slowly, I started going back to dance.
It didn't stop hurting overnight. But I wasn't carrying it alone anymore.
- Sonali

qa.q: How long had Sonali and Francis been together?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling during those two weeks?
qa.a: Sonali felt heartbroken and overwhelmed, withdrawing from breakfast, dance and friends.

qa.q: Which kinds of support helped Sonali recover?
qa.a: The mother staying close without lecturing, and friends coming over with a film and popcorn, which helped Sonali slowly return to dance.

qa.q: How might Francis have seen the breakup differently?
qa.a: Francis framed it as needing to focus on exams and let people call it mutual, possibly not realising how deeply it hurt Sonali.

grounding: The account shows a teenager withdrawing and posting cryptic lyrics after a breakup, and family and friends supporting recovery.

passage:
Librarian's note, Friday
For two weeks Maria has spent every lunch at the back table, where she used to sit with Pallavi and three others. The others eat in the canteen now; Pallavi walks past the library window without looking in. A classmate of Maria's showed me, worried, that her status says "some people show you who they are 🙂", a smile that doesn't look like one. Meanwhile she has signed up for debate, quiz and the eco club, all in one week, and was here till six on Wednesday. Today I asked if she would help me shelve returns. Halfway through the history section she said, very fast, "We were five and now I'm one," and cried into the atlas cart. I sat with her until the bell. She said she hadn't told her parents because "it's just friends". I told her it's allowed to hurt like this, and with her agreement I phoned her mother after school. Her mother is coming in on Monday; Maria has asked to keep shelving on Tuesdays.

qa.q: Who used to sit at the back table with Maria?
qa.a: Pallavi and three others used to sit there with Maria.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she said 'We were five and now I'm one'?
qa.a: Maria felt heartbroken and lonely after the group split, crying into the atlas cart; the rush of new clubs may also show she was trying to outrun the sadness.

qa.q: How did the librarian support Maria?
qa.a: The librarian gave Maria a quiet task, sat with her through the tears, said it was allowed to hurt, and with her agreement brought in her mother.

qa.q: What might the classmate who showed the status have been feeling?
qa.a: That classmate was likely worried about Maria, reading a smiley under a sad line as a sign she wasn't okay, and chose to tell an adult.

grounding: It shows a teenager after a friend-group split withdrawing, posting a cryptic status and piling on activities, and a caring adult helping bring in family support.
